terms.definition: The function that recruits, develops, and manages employees to meet organizational goals.
terms.whyItMatters: HR decisions shape staffing quality, service delivery, and culture.

terms.definition: The process of finding and attracting qualified candidates for open positions.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective recruitment ensures a business has the talent to meet its needs.

terms.definition: A systematic study of a job's duties, responsibilities, and required skills.
terms.whyItMatters: It informs hiring standards and identifies the right competencies for a role.

terms.definition: A document outlining a position's duties, qualifications, and reporting relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear descriptions guide hiring, set expectations, and reduce role confusion.

terms.definition: The process of orienting and integrating new employees into the organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong onboarding speeds productivity and conveys company values and procedures.

terms.definition: Programs that build employee skills and knowledge for current and future roles.
terms.whyItMatters: Training improves performance, cuts turnover, and prepares people for advancement.

terms.definition: A formal review of how well an employee meets job expectations.
terms.whyItMatters: Appraisals surface strengths and gaps and link development to compensation.

terms.definition: The wages, salaries, bonuses, and other financial rewards given for work.
terms.whyItMatters: Fair, competitive pay attracts talent, motivates performance, and aids retention.

terms.definition: Non-wage offerings such as health insurance, retirement plans, and paid time off.
terms.whyItMatters: Benefits influence hiring decisions and employee satisfaction.

terms.definition: Including people of different backgrounds, perspectives, and identities in the workforce.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversity improves problem-solving and reflects the customer base.

terms.definition: Managing the relationship between employers and employees, including unions and disputes.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective labor relations minimize conflict and keep the workforce productive.

terms.definition: Analyzing the current workforce and forecasting future talent needs.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures a business has the right people and skills to meet its goals.

terms.definition: Technology that stores and manages employee data and HR processes.
terms.whyItMatters: An HRIS improves efficiency and enables data-driven HR decisions.

terms.definition: (All external recruiting costs + all internal recruiting costs) divided by the number of hires made in the same period — advertising, agency fees, travel, referral bonuses and recruiter salary all belong in the numerator, so $84,000 of total spend against 24 hires is $3,500. Only completed hires count in the denominator, never openings still in process.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring-manager roleplay that asks you to justify a recruiting budget to an owner is scored on whether you divide total recruiting spend by hires rather than quoting the job-board invoice alone.

terms.definition: Calendar days from the day a requisition is approved to the day a candidate accepts the offer, averaged across openings. Its near-twin, time to hire, starts the clock later — at the day the hired person first applied — so time to fill measures the whole requisition including sourcing delay while time to hire measures only the candidate's own journey, and a 62-day time to fill can sit on top of a 19-day time to hire.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you both numbers and ask which one proves the bottleneck is job-posting approval rather than the interview loop.

terms.definition: Offers accepted divided by offers extended, times 100 — 27 acceptances on 36 offers is 75%. Declines by candidates who never received a formal offer are excluded, so the figure isolates whether pay and the closing conversation are competitive, not whether sourcing produced enough applicants.
terms.whyItMatters: In a compensation roleplay, a falling acceptance rate is the evidence that a pay range lags the market; the judge wants the ratio, not an impression that candidates seem unhappy.

terms.definition: The percentage of candidates who move from one recruiting stage to the next — 400 applicants producing 80 screens is a 20% yield, and 80 screens producing 20 interviews is 25%. Chained backward, the stage yields tell a recruiter how many applicants the top of the funnel must hold to end with a set number of hires: 5 hires at these rates requires roughly 400 applicants.
terms.whyItMatters: Hiring-plan roleplays ask how many applications a posting must attract for four openings, which is solved by multiplying the stage yields, not by guessing.

terms.definition: Number hired divided by number of applicants — 8 hires from 400 applicants is 0.02. Unlike a yield ratio, which measures one stage, this compares the two ends of the funnel, and a smaller number means a more selective process: 0.02 gives the employer far more room to be choosy than 0.50 does.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing questions pair the selection ratio with a test's validity to argue that a screening tool only adds value when the employer has many applicants per opening.

terms.definition: Resignations and retirements — separations the employee chose — divided by average headcount for the period, times 100: 18 quits against an average of 240 employees is 7.5%. Involuntary turnover uses the same denominator but counts terminations and layoffs the employer chose, and the two must be reported separately because the fixes differ: pay and management for one, hiring quality for the other.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that reports one blended turnover number is incomplete; the judge expects the voluntary share isolated before any retention spending is proposed.

terms.definition: Employees present at both the start and the end of a period, divided by the headcount at the start, times 100 — 190 of 200 starters still present is 95%. It is not simply 100 minus the turnover rate, because turnover uses average headcount and counts departures of people hired mid-period, while retention ignores anyone hired after the start date.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a turnover figure and ask for retention; subtracting from 100 is the trap, and the different denominators are the tested point.

terms.definition: Worker-days lost to unscheduled absence divided by (average number of employees times scheduled workdays), times 100 — 96 days lost across 40 employees over 20 workdays is 96/800, or 12%. Scheduled vacation and approved leave stay out of the numerator, which is why a business with generous paid time off can still post a low rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays ask you to quantify an attendance problem before proposing a policy; the ratio is what turns supervisor complaints into a defensible number.

terms.definition: (Monetary benefit of the program minus program cost) divided by program cost, times 100 — a $60,000 gain from a $20,000 course is (60,000 - 20,000)/20,000, or 200%. The benefit must be converted to dollars first, typically from reduced error rates or faster ramp time, which is the step that separates it from a satisfaction score collected at the end of class.
terms.whyItMatters: A training-proposal roleplay is scored on converting the learning gain into dollars and dividing by cost, not on describing how much participants enjoyed the session.

terms.definition: A headcount unit built from hours rather than bodies: total hours worked divided by the hours of one full-time schedule, so 2,080 annual hours or 40 weekly hours equals 1.0, and four employees at 10 hours a week together equal 1.0. Under the Affordable Care Act the full-time line is drawn at 30 hours a week or 130 a month instead of 40, so the same staff can be 22 people and 14.5 FTEs at once.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing-budget roleplays ask for labor cost per FTE, and health-coverage questions turn on the 30-hour ACA count rather than the payroll headcount.

terms.definition: An employee's pay divided by the midpoint of the assigned pay range, usually shown as a percentage: $52,000 against a $65,000 midpoint is 0.80, and $71,500 against the same midpoint is 1.10. Below 1.00 marks someone new or still developing in the job; a group average well under 1.00 across an experienced team is the standard signal that the range is being used to underpay.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-equity roleplays give a salary and a range and ask whether the person is paid fairly, which is answered with the compa-ratio and not with the raw dollar figure.

terms.definition: (Range maximum minus range minimum) divided by the minimum, times 100 — a grade running $40,000 to $60,000 has a 50% spread. Spreads widen as jobs get bigger: roughly 30 to 40% for clerical grades, 40 to 50% for professionals and 50% or more for executives, because senior jobs give a long-tenured performer more room to grow in pay without a promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Structuring a pay grade in a compensation roleplay requires setting the minimum and maximum from the midpoint and the intended spread, a calculation judges look for explicitly.

terms.definition: Pay left above the maximum of an employee's grade after a job is re-evaluated downward or a range is lowered — the salary is frozen or paid out as a lump sum instead of a base increase until the range catches up. Its opposite, a green-circled rate, sits below the grade minimum and is corrected by moving the employee up to at least the minimum, usually on a set schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: In a restructuring roleplay you must say what happens to a person whose job was downgraded; freezing base pay rather than cutting it is the answer judges expect.

terms.definition: The differential between a long-tenured employee and a newly hired peer shrinking to nothing or inverting — a five-year employee at $58,000 next to a new hire brought in at $61,000 because market rates rose faster than annual merit increases of 3%. It differs from a straight pay-equity gap in that the cause is market movement over time rather than a protected characteristic, and the fix is a market adjustment, not a discrimination remedy.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay in which top performers resign after a hiring spree is usually a compression problem, and naming the differential is what earns the point.

terms.definition: A grid whose rows are performance ratings and whose columns are quartiles of the pay range, with a percentage in each cell: an outstanding performer in the first quartile might receive 6% while the same rating in the fourth quartile receives 3%, and a below-standard rating receives 0% anywhere. The two-way design keeps high performers moving toward the midpoint while stopping anyone from being pushed past the maximum.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a rating and a compa-ratio in a roleplay, you are expected to read the correct cell and explain why two people with the same rating get different percentages.

terms.definition: Employer benefit and payroll-tax cost expressed as a percentage of base pay — $19,500 of insurance, retirement and taxes on a $65,000 salary is a 30% load, making the fully loaded cost $84,500. National figures put benefits near 31% of total compensation, which is why an offer decision compares loaded cost rather than salary alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Budgeting a new position in a roleplay is wrong if you quote only the salary; judges look for the loaded figure when the owner asks what the hire really costs.

terms.definition: A premium paid for working a less desirable schedule, set either as cents per hour or as a percentage — commonly 10% for evenings and 15% for nights, so $20.00 an hour becomes $23.00 on nights. It is not overtime: it is owed for the hours themselves regardless of weekly total, and it must be folded into the regular rate before time-and-a-half is computed, so the overtime hour is $34.50, not $30.00.
terms.whyItMatters: Payroll questions test whether the differential enters the regular rate before the overtime multiplier, a step candidates routinely skip.

terms.definition: An employer contribution formula that exempts a retirement plan from annual nondiscrimination testing: the basic version matches 100% of the first 3% of pay an employee defers plus 50% of the next 2%, capping the employer at 4% of pay, and the alternative is a 3% nonelective contribution to every eligible employee whether they defer or not. Safe harbor money must be fully vested immediately, unlike a discretionary match.
terms.whyItMatters: A benefits roleplay for a small business with highly paid owners turns on the safe harbor as the way to let owners defer fully, and the judge expects the formula.

terms.definition: Ownership of employer retirement contributions earned in slices — commonly 20% after two years of service and 20% each year thereafter, reaching 100% at six years, so an employee leaving at year four keeps 60%. The alternative, cliff vesting, gives 0% until a single date and 100% on it, capped by law at three years for defined contribution plans; employee deferrals are always 100% vested from the first dollar under either schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked in a roleplay what a departing employee takes with them, you must apply the schedule to the years of service instead of assuming the whole account balance.

terms.definition: The right of a worker leaving an employer with 20 or more employees to keep the group health plan for up to 18 months, extended to 29 months for disability and 36 months for a spouse or dependent after divorce or death. The qualified beneficiary has 60 days to elect and may be charged 102% of the full premium — the employer subsidy ends, which is why the monthly cost often quadruples.
terms.whyItMatters: A separation roleplay is scored on stating the election window and that the former employee now pays the full premium plus the 2% administrative charge.

terms.definition: The Affordable Care Act rule that an employer averaging 50 or more full-time-equivalent employees in the prior year must offer minimum essential coverage to at least 95% of full-time employees and their dependents or owe a per-employee penalty. Full time here means 30 hours a week or 130 a month, and coverage is affordable only if the employee's share of self-only premium stays under roughly 9.5% of household income as annually indexed.
terms.whyItMatters: A growing-business roleplay that asks whether hiring the 50th worker changes obligations depends on the FTE count and the 30-hour line, not on the payroll headcount.

terms.definition: The mechanism that ties a state unemployment tax rate to an employer's own history of benefit charges — an employer that has laid off heavily may pay several times the rate of one that has not, on the same taxable wage base. Federal unemployment tax is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, reduced by a 5.4% credit to a net 0.6%, or $42 per employee, when the state account is in good standing.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost questions about layoffs versus reduced hours turn on the rating consequence, which competitors usually miss by treating unemployment tax as a fixed cost.

terms.definition: Requires equal pay for men and women performing jobs of equal skill, effort and responsibility under similar working conditions in the same establishment, and unlike a Title VII claim it needs no proof of intent. An employer escapes liability only through one of four defenses — a seniority system, a merit system, a system measuring quantity or quality of production, or any factor other than sex — and may never correct a gap by lowering the higher-paid worker's wage.
terms.whyItMatters: A pay-audit roleplay is scored on naming a permitted defense for the differential rather than asserting that the two jobs simply have different titles.

terms.definition: Protects workers aged 40 and over at employers with 20 or more employees, so a 38-year-old passed over for a 55-year-old has no claim under it and neither does a 12-person shop. Unlike Title VII, it protects only the older side of the line, meaning favoring a 60-year-old over a 45-year-old is not unlawful even though both are inside the protected class.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring-decision roleplay that mentions a candidate's age needs the 40-and-over line and the 20-employee threshold before you can say whether the statute even applies.

terms.definition: Sets the conditions under which a worker 40 or older can validly waive an age claim in exchange for severance: at least 21 days to consider the agreement, a 7-day period to revoke after signing, written advice to consult an attorney, and consideration beyond what was already owed. In a group layoff the consideration period stretches to 45 days and the employer must disclose the job titles and ages of everyone selected and everyone spared.
terms.whyItMatters: Drafting a severance offer in a downsizing roleplay is incomplete without the review and revocation periods, and the group-layoff disclosure is the detail judges reward.

terms.term: Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA)
terms.definition: Guarantees reemployment to a worker returning from military service, capped at five years of cumulative absence from one employer, with the return application due within 1 day for service under 31 days, 14 days for service of 31 to 180 days, and 90 days beyond that. The escalator principle puts the returning worker in the position they would have reached had they never left, not merely the job they held on departure.
terms.whyItMatters: A reinstatement roleplay is scored on the escalator principle — offering the old job back at the old pay is the wrong answer when promotions occurred meanwhile.

terms.definition: The employment eligibility verification record required of every U.S. employer by the Immigration Reform and Control Act: the employee completes Section 1 no later than the first day of work for pay, and the employer examines original documents and completes Section 2 within three business days of that start. The form is retained three years after hire or one year after termination, whichever is later, and is kept apart from the personnel file.
terms.whyItMatters: An onboarding roleplay that lists paperwork must place this inside the three-business-day window, a deadline competitors routinely confuse with the first payroll run.

terms.definition: The deadline for bringing a federal discrimination charge — 180 calendar days from the discriminatory act, extended to 300 days in a deferral state that has its own fair employment agency covering the same conduct. Filing the charge is a prerequisite to suit, and once the agency issues a right-to-sue notice the employee has 90 days to file in court, a separate and much shorter clock.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint-handling roleplays test whether you know an internal investigation does not pause the statutory clock, and the 180/300-day split is the point being probed.

terms.definition: A narrow statutory defense allowing an employer to hire on the basis of sex, religion, national origin or age when that characteristic is reasonably necessary to the essence of the business — an actor's sex for a specific role, or a mandatory retirement age for airline pilots. It can never justify a race-based decision, and it differs from business necessity, which defends a neutral rule that happens to screen out a group, whereas this defends an openly stated preference.
terms.whyItMatters: In a staffing roleplay involving a customer preference for one sex, the tested answer is that customer preference is not a valid basis for this defense.

terms.definition: A contract term requiring bargaining-unit employees to join the union or pay fees as a condition of continued employment — a union shop allows a grace period of 30 days after hire, shortened to 7 days in construction. Section 14(b) of the Taft-Hartley Act lets a state outlaw such clauses entirely, which is what a right-to-work state does, leaving the union obligated to represent employees who pay nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A labor-relations roleplay set in a right-to-work state is scored on knowing the clause is unenforceable there while the duty of fair representation continues.

terms.definition: Conduct prohibited by the National Labor Relations Act — Section 8(a) lists the five employer violations including interference with organizing, domination of a labor organization, discrimination for union activity and refusal to bargain in good faith, while Section 8(b) lists the union counterparts such as coercion of employees and secondary boycotts. A charge must reach the Board within six months of the conduct under Section 10(b).
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect you to identify which subsection a supervisor's threat falls under during an organizing-campaign roleplay, not merely to call the behavior unfair.

terms.definition: The secret-ballot vote that decides union representation: a petition requires authorization cards from at least 30% of the proposed bargaining unit, and certification follows a simple majority of ballots actually cast, not of the unit — 40 votes for out of 70 cast in a 100-person unit certifies the union. A valid election bars another for 12 months, and a resulting contract bars one for up to three years.
terms.whyItMatters: Organizing roleplays test the 30% showing of interest against the majority needed to win, a pair of numbers competitors frequently collapse into one.

terms.definition: A selection interview in which every candidate receives the same predetermined questions in the same order and answers are scored against written anchors, rather than the interviewer following the conversation wherever it goes. Research places its predictive validity near .51 against roughly .38 for the unstructured version, and the fixed script is also what makes the process defensible when a rejected applicant alleges disparate treatment.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay asking how to make interviews fairer is answered by fixing the question set and the scoring key, not by adding a second interviewer.

terms.definition: An appraisal method that requires managers to sort employees into fixed proportions — often 20% top, 70% middle and 10% bottom — regardless of how the group actually performed, so a strong team must still produce a bottom 10%. Its counterpart, a behaviorally anchored rating scale, rates each person against written behavior standards with no quota, which is why the two produce different outcomes for the same identical team.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect the quota objection when a roleplay asks whether to adopt ranking: rating a high-performing department this way forces an unfair low rating.

terms.definition: A rating form whose points are each defined by a real example of observable behavior — a 5 might read greets every guest within thirty seconds while a 2 reads acknowledges guests only after they approach — built from critical incidents gathered from people who do the job. A plain graphic rating scale labels the same points only excellent through poor, which is why two managers can rate identical behavior differently on it.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay complains that appraisals are inconsistent between supervisors, the tested fix is anchoring each scale point in described behavior.

terms.definition: A documented escalation applied to correctable conduct — typically verbal warning, written warning, final written warning or suspension, then termination — with each step recorded, dated and acknowledged so the record shows notice was given. It is deliberately bypassed for gross misconduct such as theft, violence or safety sabotage, where immediate termination is appropriate, and skipping steps for ordinary conduct is what makes a later discharge look pretextual.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay about a chronically late employee is scored on naming the step reached and what documentation exists, not on describing a conversation.

terms.definition: A structured conversation held with a current, valued employee while there is still time to act, asking what would make them leave and what keeps them — the findings can change that person's situation. An exit interview asks similar questions after the resignation is submitted, so its value is only aggregate trend data for future employees; the timing is the whole difference between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that proposes only exit interviews concedes every departure; judges look for the forward-looking conversation with people still on the payroll.

terms.definition: Redesigning a job by loading it vertically — handing the employee planning, decision-making and quality-checking authority previously held by a supervisor, which deepens responsibility. Job enlargement instead loads horizontally, adding more tasks at the same level of authority, and job rotation moves the person between existing jobs without changing any of them; only enrichment changes the amount of control the worker holds.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to motivate a bored experienced employee in a roleplay, adding more of the same tasks is the trap answer; the tested one is giving away supervisory decisions.

terms.definition: The half of a job-analysis output that describes the person rather than the work — required education, licensure, years of experience, skills and physical requirements. Its companion, the job description, lists the duties, reporting relationship and working conditions of the position itself; a screening decision must be traceable to the specification, because a requirement that appears nowhere in it is very hard to defend as job related.
terms.whyItMatters: Building a posting in a hiring roleplay is scored on separating what the job does from what the person must bring, which is where invented requirements get caught.

terms.definition: The degree of discretionary effort and psychological commitment a worker brings to the organization's goals, measured through driver surveys covering manager quality, recognition and growth. It is not job satisfaction: a comfortable employee can be entirely satisfied and contribute nothing extra, which is why engagement tracks against productivity and turnover while satisfaction alone often does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to build stronger employer-employee relationships expects engagement drivers and a measurement plan rather than a morale-boosting event.

terms.definition: The set of unwritten mutual expectations between employer and worker — promotion prospects, schedule flexibility, job security, loyalty — that no signed document records but both sides act on. Breaching it, such as quietly ending remote work after implying it was permanent, damages trust and drives resignations even when nothing legally binding was broken.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay describes an angry workforce after a policy change that violated no written rule, this is the concept that names what actually went wrong.

terms.definition: The stepped route a complaint travels under a collective bargaining agreement — usually the immediate supervisor, then department management with a union steward, then a company-wide review, ending in binding arbitration by a neutral third party whose decision both sides accepted in advance. Each step carries its own filing deadline, and missing one can forfeit the claim regardless of merit.
terms.whyItMatters: A union-workplace roleplay is scored on routing the complaint through the contract's steps rather than settling it informally with the employee.

terms.definition: The function that handles the individual relationship between a business and its non-union workforce — investigations, conduct issues, policy interpretation and conflict between coworkers. Labor relations, by contrast, deals with the collective relationship governed by a negotiated contract with a certified union, so a non-union employer has the first function and none of the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about building positive employer-employee relationships in a non-union business belong to this function, and misnaming it as labor relations costs the point.
